subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: When a rock formed, it contained nuclei of a radioactive isotope with decay constant λ but no nuclei of its stable daughter isotope. Each decay produces one daughter nucleus, which stays in the rock. The ratio of the number of daughter nuclei to the number of undecayed nuclei of the radioactive isotope in the rock is now r. Which expression gives the age of the rock?
optionWhy: If P parent nuclei remain, there are D = rP daughter nuclei, and each came from one parent nucleus that decayed. So the rock started with N₀ = P + rP = P(1 + r) parent nuclei and has N = P now. From ln(N/N₀) = −λt, t = (1/λ)ln(N₀/N) = (1/λ) ln(1 + r).
A student who counts half-lives, n = ln(1 + r)/ln 2 (since N₀/N = 2ⁿ = 1 + r), and then takes the half-life to be 1/λ picks this. The half-life is t₁/₂ = (ln 2)/λ, so t = n t₁/₂ = (1/λ) ln(1 + r).
A student who uses the fraction that has decayed, D/(P + D) = r/(1 + r), as the fraction remaining, N/N₀, picks this. The fraction remaining is P/(P + D) = 1/(1 + r), so N₀/N = 1 + r.

A student who thinks nuclei decay at a steady rate, half in one half-life t₁/₂ = (ln 2)/λ and the rest in the next, sets the fraction decayed, r/(1 + r), equal to t/(2t₁/₂) and picks this. The number of decays per unit time falls as the number of parent nuclei falls, so N = N₀e^(−λt).
questions.explain: If P parent nuclei remain, there are D = rP daughter nuclei, and each came from one parent nucleus that decayed. So the rock started with N₀ = P + rP = P(1 + r) parent nuclei and has N = P now. From ln(N/N₀) = −λt, t = (1/λ)ln(N₀/N) = (1/λ) ln(1 + r).
questions.working: If P parent nuclei remain and D = rP daughter nuclei are present, each daughter came from one decayed parent, so N₀ = P + D = P(1 + r) and N = P. ln(N/N₀) = −λt ⇒ t = (1/λ)ln(N₀/N) = (1/λ) ln(1 + r). Errors: counting half-lives n = ln(1 + r)/ln 2 and taking t₁/₂ = 1/λ → (1/λ)ln(1 + r)/ln 2; fraction decayed D/(P + D) = r/(1 + r) used as N/N₀ → (1/λ) ln(1 + 1/r); steady decay rate (straight-line fall, half gone in t₁/₂ = (ln 2)/λ, all gone in 2t₁/₂): D/(P + D) = t/(2t₁/₂) ⇒ t = 2r ln 2/(λ(1 + r)).

questions.q: A nucleus at rest undergoes alpha decay. The alpha particle, of mass m, moves off with speed v, and the new nucleus formed has mass M. All of the energy released in the decay becomes kinetic energy of the alpha particle and the new nucleus, and both speeds are much less than the speed of light. Which expression gives the energy released in the decay?
options: ½mv²(M+m)/M
½(M+m)v²
mv²
½mv²
optionWhy: The total momentum is zero before the decay, so afterward MV = mv and the new nucleus recoils with speed V = mv/M. The energy released is the total kinetic energy: ½mv² + ½M(mv/M)² = ½mv²(1 + m/M) = ½mv²(M+m)/M, a little more than the alpha particle's own kinetic energy.

A student who thinks the two particles fly apart with equal speeds picks this, giving the new nucleus speed v as well. Their momenta must be equal in magnitude, so the much more massive new nucleus moves far more slowly, at mv/M.

A student who thinks the energy is shared equally picks this, giving the new nucleus the same kinetic energy as the alpha particle, ½mv². Because the momenta are equal in magnitude, the kinetic energies are in the inverse ratio of the masses, so the new nucleus has only m/M of the alpha particle's kinetic energy.

A student who treats the new nucleus as staying at rest picks this, counting only the alpha particle's kinetic energy. The total momentum is zero after the decay as before, so the new nucleus recoils with momentum equal in magnitude to the alpha particle's and carries some of the energy released.
questions.explain: The total momentum is zero before the decay, so afterward MV = mv and the new nucleus recoils with speed V = mv/M. The energy released is the total kinetic energy: ½mv² + ½M(mv/M)² = ½mv²(1 + m/M) = ½mv²(M+m)/M, a little more than the alpha particle's own kinetic energy.
questions.working: Momentum: 0 = mv − MV, so V = mv/M. Energy released Q = ½mv² + ½MV² = ½mv² + ½m²v²/M = ½mv²(M+m)/M. Check (m = 4.00 u, M = 222 u, v = 1.52 × 10⁷ m/s): Q = 7.81 × 10⁻¹³ J, and momentum and energy both balance. Errors: equal speeds → ½(M+m)v²; equal kinetic energies (½mv² each) → mv²; new nucleus at rest → ½mv².

questions.q: Samples of two isotopes, X and Y, initially contain equal numbers of nuclei. The decay constant of Y is twice the decay constant of X. What fraction of the original Y nuclei remains undecayed after a time equal to the half-life of X?
optionWhy: λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂, so doubling λ halves the half-life: Y's half-life is half of X's. In a time equal to X's half-life, Y goes through two of its half-lives, so (1/2)² = 0.25 of the Y nuclei remain.
A student who gives the fraction that has decayed picks this. After two half-lives of Y, 0.75 of the Y nuclei have decayed and 0.25 remain.

A student who thinks a larger decay constant means a longer half-life picks this, making Y's half-life twice X's; Y would then have gone through half a half-life, leaving (1/2)^(1/2) = 0.71. Doubling λ halves the half-life.

A student who treats decay as steady picks this: X loses half its nuclei in its half-life, so Y, decaying twice as fast, would lose all of them. Decay is exponential: Y loses half of its remaining nuclei in each of its half-lives, leaving 0.25.
questions.explain: λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂, so doubling λ halves the half-life: Y's half-life is half of X's. In a time equal to X's half-life, Y goes through two of its half-lives, so (1/2)² = 0.25 of the Y nuclei remain.
questions.working: t₁/₂Y = ln 2/λ_Y = ln 2/(2λ_X) = t₁/₂X/2. Time t = t₁/₂X = 2t₁/₂Y → N/N₀ = (1/2)² = 0.25. Errors: decayed fraction 0.75; half-life doubled → 2^(−1/2) = 0.71; linear → 1 − 2 × 0.5 = 0.

questions.q: The table shows the half-lives of four radioactive isotopes. Which claim is supported by the data in the table?
options: After 9.0 × 10⁹ years, no uranium-238 nuclei remain, just as no iodine-131 nuclei remain after 16 days.
Every iodine-131 nucleus lasts exactly 8.0 days, and every carbon-14 nucleus lasts exactly 5730 years.
After 1 year, under 10⁻¹² of iodine-131 nuclei remain, but over 99.9% of carbon-14 nuclei do.
A sample with half as many carbon-14 or iodine-131 nuclei would have half the half-life shown.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a sample is used up in two half-lives picks this. 9.0 × 10⁹ years is two half-lives of uranium-238 and 16 days is two half-lives of iodine-131; after two half-lives one-quarter of the nuclei remain undecayed.

A student who takes the half-life to be the lifetime of each nucleus picks this. The time at which one nucleus decays cannot be predicted; in one half-life, half of a large number of nuclei decay, some soon after the start and some much later.

One year is 365/8.0 ≈ 46 half-lives of iodine-131, so the fraction remaining is about (1/2)⁴⁶ ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁴, under 10⁻¹². One year is 1/5730 of carbon-14's half-life, so the fraction remaining is (1/2)^(1/5730) ≈ 0.99988, over 99.9%. Half-lives of different isotopes differ enormously.

A student who thinks the half-life depends on the amount of material picks this. The half-life is a property of the isotope: 5730 years for any sample of carbon-14 and 8.0 days for any sample of iodine-131. Half as many nuclei give half as many decays per second, not a shorter half-life.
questions.explain: One year is 365/8.0 ≈ 46 half-lives of iodine-131, so the fraction remaining is about (1/2)⁴⁶ ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁴, under 10⁻¹². One year is 1/5730 of carbon-14's half-life, so the fraction remaining is (1/2)^(1/5730) ≈ 0.99988, over 99.9%. Half-lives of different isotopes differ enormously.
questions.working: Iodine-131: 365/8.0 = 45.6 half-lives → (1/2)^45.6 = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁴ remaining (< 10⁻¹²). Carbon-14: 1/5730 of a half-life → 2^(−1/5730) = 0.99988 remaining (> 99.9%). Uranium-238: 9.0 × 10⁹ y = 2 half-lives → 1/4 remains; iodine-131 after 16 days = 2 half-lives → 1/4 remains.

questions.q: For a radioactive isotope, the graph shows ln(N/N₀) as a function of time t, where N₀ is the initial number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample and N is the number remaining. For one sample of this isotope, N/N₀ = 0.30 now. How long ago was N equal to N₀?
options: 35 days
60 days
26 days
15 days
optionWhy: A student who uses a steady-rate model, N = N₀(1 − λt), picks this: t = (1 − 0.30)/0.020 day⁻¹ = 35 days. Decay is exponential: use ln(N/N₀) = −λt, which gives 60 days.
ln(0.30) = −1.20. The line reaches ln(N/N₀) = −1.20 at t = 60 days. (Equivalently, the slope gives λ = 2.0/100 days = 0.020 day⁻¹, and t = −ln(0.30)/λ = 1.20/0.020 day⁻¹ = 60 days.)
A student who uses the common logarithm picks this: log(0.30) = −0.52, which the line reaches at 26 days. The graph is of the natural logarithm; ln(0.30) = −1.20, reached at 60 days.

A student who reads the vertical axis as N/N₀ itself picks this, finding where the line reaches −0.30. The axis shows ln(N/N₀), so the ratio 0.30 must first be converted: ln(0.30) = −1.20, reached at 60 days.
questions.explain: ln(0.30) = −1.20. The line reaches ln(N/N₀) = −1.20 at t = 60 days. (Equivalently, the slope gives λ = 2.0/100 days = 0.020 day⁻¹, and t = −ln(0.30)/λ = 1.20/0.020 day⁻¹ = 60 days.)
questions.working: Slope = −2.0/100 days → λ = 0.020 day⁻¹. ln(0.30) = −1.204 → t = 1.204/0.020 = 60.2 days ≈ 60 days (read directly from the line at −1.20). Errors: linear (1 − 0.30)/0.020 = 35; log₁₀: 0.523/0.020 = 26; reading −0.30 on the axis: 0.30/0.020 = 15.

questions.q: A detector records the number of decays from a sample of a long-lived isotope (half-life 30 years) in ten successive 10-second intervals. The bar chart shows the results. Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: The counts vary irregularly about a steady average, as expected when decays occur at random.
The detector must be faulty, since every radioactive sample decays at one fixed, steady rate.
The counts vary because the half-life of the sample changes as its number of nuclei decreases.
The counts vary because the temperature of the room changed during the measurements.
optionWhy: The counts range from 41 to 58 with no upward or downward trend. In a few minutes a sample with a 30-year half-life loses a negligible fraction of its nuclei, so the average rate is steady; the irregular variation is what random decay predicts, since the number of nuclei that happen to decay in each interval varies by chance.

A student who expects exactly equal counts in equal intervals picks this. Each decay is a random event, so counts of about 50 per interval are expected to vary by several counts either way even with a perfect detector.

A student who thinks the half-life depends on the amount of material picks this. The half-life is fixed for the isotope, and in a few minutes the number of nuclei in a sample with a 30-year half-life hardly changes.

A student who thinks conditions such as temperature change the decay rate picks this. Everyday temperature changes affect atoms, not nuclei, and nothing in the data points to a temperature change; the variation is the random scatter of decay.
questions.explain: The counts range from 41 to 58 with no upward or downward trend. In a few minutes a sample with a 30-year half-life loses a negligible fraction of its nuclei, so the average rate is steady; the irregular variation is what random decay predicts, since the number of nuclei that happen to decay in each interval varies by chance.

questions.q: The bar chart shows the total binding energy of each of two nuclei, X and Y, and the total binding energy of the fragments that each nucleus would form by fission. Which claim is supported by the chart?
options: Fission of X would need an energy input, since X's fragments have a greater total binding energy than X.
Neither fission would need an energy input, since splitting a nucleus releases energy.
Both fissions would need an energy input, since energy is needed to break a nucleus apart.
Fission of Y would need an energy input, since Y's fragments have less total binding energy than Y.
optionWhy: A student who thinks binding energy is energy stored in a nucleus picks this, reasoning that the fragments must be given the extra 180 MeV. More binding energy means the fragments are more tightly bound and have less mass than X, so fission of X releases about 180 MeV.

A student who thinks every fission releases energy picks this. The chart shows Y's fragments with less total binding energy than Y (321 MeV compared with 342 MeV), so they have more mass than Y and energy must be supplied to form them.

A student who thinks splitting anything always costs energy picks this. Fission forms smaller nuclei, not separate nucleons. X's fragments have more total binding energy than X, so they have less mass and the fission of X releases energy.

Nucleon number is conserved, so fragments with less total binding energy (321 MeV compared with 342 MeV for Y) are less tightly bound and have more total mass than Y. Their extra rest energy, about 21 MeV, must be supplied, so the fission of Y needs an energy input. X's fragments have more binding energy than X (1970 MeV compared with 1790 MeV), so fission of X releases energy.
questions.explain: Nucleon number is conserved, so fragments with less total binding energy (321 MeV compared with 342 MeV for Y) are less tightly bound and have more total mass than Y. Their extra rest energy, about 21 MeV, must be supplied, so the fission of Y needs an energy input. X's fragments have more binding energy than X (1970 MeV compared with 1790 MeV), so fission of X releases energy.

questions.q: A nucleus at rest undergoes alpha decay. The new nucleus formed has about 50 times the mass of the alpha particle. How do the kinetic energies of the alpha particle and the new nucleus compare just after the decay?
options: They are equal, since the energy released is shared out equally between them.
The new nucleus's is much greater, since the two move apart at equal speeds.
Their total is zero, since the total kinetic energy before the decay was zero.
The alpha particle's is much greater, as their momenta are equal in size.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the energy is shared equally picks this. Conservation of momentum fixes how the energy is divided: with equal momenta, K = p²/(2m) gives the lighter alpha particle about 50 times the kinetic energy of the new nucleus.

A student who thinks the particles move apart at equal speeds picks this, then uses K = ½mv² to give the heavier nucleus more energy. Equal speeds would give the new nucleus 50 times the momentum of the alpha particle, so momentum would not be conserved.

A student who treats kinetic energy like momentum, as able to cancel, picks this. Kinetic energy is a scalar and cannot be negative; the products share the energy released, so their total kinetic energy is positive. It is the total momentum that stays zero.
The total momentum stays zero, so the two momenta have equal magnitudes p. Kinetic energy K = p²/(2m), so with equal p the particle with about 1/50 of the mass has about 50 times the kinetic energy.
questions.explain: The total momentum stays zero, so the two momenta have equal magnitudes p. Kinetic energy K = p²/(2m), so with equal p the particle with about 1/50 of the mass has about 50 times the kinetic energy.

questions.q: When two light nuclei fuse, energy is released. A student claims that this energy comes from some of the protons and neutrons being converted into energy. Which is the best evaluation of the student's claim?
options: It is correct; the energy released is the rest energy of the nucleons that disappear.
It is incorrect; mass cannot change, so the energy comes from the nuclei's motion before fusing.
It is incorrect; the number of nucleons is unchanged, and the products have less mass.
It is incorrect; the energy is binding energy that was stored in the nuclei before they fused.
optionWhy: A student who thinks 'mass converted into energy' means particles vanish picks this. The nucleon numbers balance in every nuclear reaction; in ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n there are 5 nucleons on each side. The mass lost (0.019 u) is a small fraction of one nucleon's mass.

A student who applies conservation of mass from chemistry picks this. In nuclear reactions the total mass does change measurably, and the energy released, far more than the kinetic energy the nuclei had before they fused, equals the decrease in mass times c².

Nucleon number is conserved in every nuclear reaction, so no protons or neutrons disappear. The products of the fusion are more tightly bound and have slightly less total mass than the reactants; this decrease in mass, times c², is the energy released.

A student who thinks binding energy is energy stored in a nucleus picks this. Binding energy is the energy needed to pull a nucleus apart. The product of fusion has more binding energy than the reactants, which is why it has less mass and energy is released.
questions.explain: Nucleon number is conserved in every nuclear reaction, so no protons or neutrons disappear. The products of the fusion are more tightly bound and have slightly less total mass than the reactants; this decrease in mass, times c², is the energy released.

questions.q: A sample contains 8.0 g of a radioactive isotope whose half-life is 5.3 years. What mass of the isotope has decayed after 12 years?
optionWhy: A student who takes the fraction found, e^(−λt) = 0.21, to be the fraction that has decayed picks this. e^(−λt) = N/N₀ is the fraction remaining, so 1 − 0.21 = 0.79 of the sample has decayed: 6.3 g.
λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂ = 0.693/(5.3 yr) = 0.131 yr⁻¹, so the fraction remaining is e^(−(0.131 yr⁻¹)(12 yr)) = 0.21. The mass remaining is 8.0 g × 0.21 = 1.7 g, so 8.0 g − 1.7 g = 6.3 g has decayed.
A student who uses λ = 1/t₁/₂ = 0.189 yr⁻¹ picks this: e^(−12/5.3) = 0.10 remains. The decay constant is λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂ = 0.131 yr⁻¹, which leaves 0.21 of the sample.
A student who uses the log key, log 2 = 0.301, in place of ln 2 = 0.693 picks this: λ = 0.057 yr⁻¹ leaves 0.51 of the sample. The decay equations use natural logarithms: λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂.
questions.explain: λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂ = 0.693/(5.3 yr) = 0.131 yr⁻¹, so the fraction remaining is e^(−(0.131 yr⁻¹)(12 yr)) = 0.21. The mass remaining is 8.0 g × 0.21 = 1.7 g, so 8.0 g − 1.7 g = 6.3 g has decayed.
questions.working: λ = (ln 2)/t₁/₂ = 0.693/(5.3 yr) = 0.131 yr⁻¹. Fraction remaining: e^(−λt) = e^(−(0.131)(12)) = e^(−1.57) = 0.208. Mass remaining 8.0 g × 0.208 = 1.67 g, so mass decayed = 8.0 g − 1.67 g = 6.33 g ≈ 6.3 g. (0.208 taken as the fraction decayed: 1.7 g; λ = 1/t₁/₂: 7.2 g; log instead of ln: 4.0 g.)

questions.q: An isotope has decay constant λ. A sample of the isotope contains N undecayed nuclei at a time t after the sample was prepared. Which expression gives the number N₀ of nuclei of the isotope that the sample contained when it was prepared?
options: Ne^(λt)
Ne^(−λt)
optionWhy: From N = N₀e^(−λt), N₀ = N/e^(−λt) = Ne^(λt). The exponent is positive, so N₀ is larger than N, as it must be.

A student who applies the decay equation with N and N₀ exchanged picks this. It gives a value smaller than N, but the sample had more nuclei when it was prepared; solving N = N₀e^(−λt) for N₀ gives Ne^(λt).
A student who uses a steady-rate model, N = N₀(1 − λt), picks this. Decay is exponential, not linear: the number decaying per unit time falls as the sample shrinks, so N = N₀e^(−λt).
A student who treats λ as if it were the half-life picks this, doubling N once for every 'λ' of elapsed time. λ is a probability per unit time (units s⁻¹), not a time; the half-life is (ln 2)/λ.
questions.explain: From N = N₀e^(−λt), N₀ = N/e^(−λt) = Ne^(λt). The exponent is positive, so N₀ is larger than N, as it must be.
questions.working: N = N₀e^(−λt) → N₀ = Ne^(λt). Errors: roles swapped → Ne^(−λt) < N; linear model N = N₀(1 − λt) → N/(1 − λt); λ used as a half-life → N·2^(t/λ).

questions.q: The table shows the number of neutrons in each of six isotopes of carbon (each has 6 protons) and how each isotope decays. Which claim is supported by the data in the table?
options: Carbon isotopes with more neutrons than the stable ones decay by β⁺.
Every unstable isotope of carbon decays by the same process.
Each carbon nucleus decays by β⁺ or β⁻, with the type chosen at random.
Carbon isotopes with more neutrons than the stable ones undergo β⁻ decay.
optionWhy: A student who thinks β⁺ decay turns a neutron into a proton expects neutron-rich isotopes to use it and picks this. The table shows carbon-14 and carbon-15, which have extra neutrons, decaying by β⁻.
A student who thinks the decay type belongs to the element picks this. The table shows two processes, β⁺ for carbon-10 and carbon-11 and β⁻ for carbon-14 and carbon-15.

A student who thinks the type of decay is random picks this. The table gives a single decay type for each isotope, and two isotopes are stable, so the type is set by the isotope, not chosen at random.

The stable isotopes have 6 and 7 neutrons. The isotopes with more (8 and 9) decay by β⁻, and those with fewer (4 and 5) decay by β⁺. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, which suits a nucleus with extra neutrons.
questions.explain: The stable isotopes have 6 and 7 neutrons. The isotopes with more (8 and 9) decay by β⁻, and those with fewer (4 and 5) decay by β⁺. In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton, which suits a nucleus with extra neutrons.

questions.q: Each beta-minus decay of a particular isotope releases the same total amount of energy. However, the emitted electrons are observed to have a range of kinetic energies, from nearly zero up to a maximum value. Which claim is best supported by this observation?
options: Another emitted particle, the antineutrino, carries off the rest of the energy.
The electrons come from different orbits of the atom, which have different energies.
Energy is not conserved in beta decay, since mass and energy are converted there.
The electrons were already inside the nucleus, each with a different energy.
optionWhy: If the released energy is always the same but the electron's share varies, another product must carry the rest in each decay. In β⁻ decay that product is the antineutrino, which is uncharged and interacts very little with matter, so it escapes unnoticed.

A student who thinks beta particles are orbiting electrons picks this. The electrons are emitted by the nucleus, where a neutron changes into a proton; the atom's electron energy levels do not set their energies.

A student who thinks mass-energy conversion suspends energy conservation picks this. Energy is conserved in every decay once mass-energy is included; the missing energy is carried away by the antineutrino.

A student who thinks a neutron is a proton and an electron joined together picks this. The nucleus contains no electrons; the electron is produced in the decay, and it shares the released energy with the antineutrino.
questions.explain: If the released energy is always the same but the electron's share varies, another product must carry the rest in each decay. In β⁻ decay that product is the antineutrino, which is uncharged and interacts very little with matter, so it escapes unnoticed.
questions.working: Fixed total energy released per decay; variable electron kinetic energy → the remainder must go to another emitted product. In β⁻ decay: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄; the antineutrino takes the difference (the recoiling nucleus takes a very small share).

questions.q: A student writes this equation for a decay of carbon-14: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + e⁺ + ν. Which is the best evidence that the equation cannot describe a real decay?
options: Nucleon number: the total is 14 before the decay but 15 after.
Lepton number: a positron must be emitted with an antineutrino.
Mass: the products have less mass than the carbon-14 nucleus.
Charge: the total is +6e before the decay but +8e after it.
optionWhy: A student who counts the positron as a nucleon picks this. The positron and neutrino have nucleon number 0, so there are 14 nucleons on each side.
A student who pairs the positron with the antineutrino picks this. In beta-plus decay a positron is emitted with a neutrino, as written; the fault in the equation is the charge.

A student who thinks mass must be conserved picks this. The products of every decay have less mass than the original nucleus; that loss of mass is the source of the energy released, not a reason the decay is impossible.

Before: carbon, charge +6e. After: nitrogen +7e plus the positron +e plus the uncharged neutrino, total +8e. Charge is not conserved, so the decay cannot happen as written. (Nucleon number, 14, is balanced, and so is lepton number: positron −1 plus neutrino +1 gives 0.)
questions.explain: Before: carbon, charge +6e. After: nitrogen +7e plus the positron +e plus the uncharged neutrino, total +8e. Charge is not conserved, so the decay cannot happen as written. (Nucleon number, 14, is balanced, and so is lepton number: positron −1 plus neutrino +1 gives 0.)
questions.working: Charge: 6e → 7e + e + 0 = 8e (not conserved). Nucleon number: 14 → 14 + 0 + 0 (conserved). Lepton number: e⁺ (−1) + ν (+1) = 0 (balanced). So charge is the violated law; the real decay of carbon-14 is ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + e⁻ + ν̄.

questions.q: The chart shows neutron number N against proton number Z. Starting from the nucleus marked with a dot, four arrows (one of them a loop back to the same nucleus) are meant to show the change produced by each of the four types of decay, as labelled. One of the four is drawn incorrectly. Which one?
options: Arrow 1
Arrow 2
Arrow 3
Arrow 4
optionWhy: A student who thinks alpha decay lowers the proton number by 4 and the nucleon number by 2 picks this. The α arrow correctly goes 2 steps left and 2 steps down: the alpha particle removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

In β⁺ decay a proton changes into a neutron, so Z falls by 1 and N rises by 1: the arrow should go one step to the left and one step up. The arrow labelled β⁺ goes one step left with no change in N, the change that losing a proton would make.

A student who thinks the changed nucleon is lost from the nucleus in beta decay expects β⁻ decay to lower N by 1 and leave Z unchanged, so the diagonal β⁻ arrow looks wrong. (The same belief makes the drawn β⁺ arrow, one step left with N unchanged, look right.) In β⁻ decay a neutron becomes a proton: Z rises by 1 and N falls by 1, exactly as drawn.
A student who thinks gamma decay changes the nucleus picks this. Gamma decay leaves Z and N unchanged, so a loop back to the same nucleus is correct.
questions.explain: In β⁺ decay a proton changes into a neutron, so Z falls by 1 and N rises by 1: the arrow should go one step to the left and one step up. The arrow labelled β⁺ goes one step left with no change in N, the change that losing a proton would make.
questions.working: Start (Z, N) = (84, 128). α: (−2, −2) → (82, 126), drawn correctly. β⁻: (+1, −1) → (85, 127), correct. β⁺ should be (−1, +1) → (83, 129); drawn (−1, 0) → (83, 128): incorrect. γ: no change, loop: correct.

questions.q: The table shows the charge and mass of four particles that can be emitted when nuclei decay. One entry in the table is incorrect. Which row contains the incorrect entry?
options: Row 1
Row 2
Row 3
Row 4
optionWhy: A positron has charge +e, as listed, but it has the same mass as an electron, about 0.00055 u, not about 1 u. A mass of about 1 u is that of a proton or a neutron.
A student who thinks every nucleon carries charge +e picks this, expecting +4e for the alpha particle. Only its two protons are charged, so +2e is correct, and its mass of about 4 u is also correct.
A student who thinks a neutrino is a kind of neutron picks this, expecting a mass of about 1 u. A neutrino has no charge and negligible mass, as listed.
A student who thinks antiparticles are always charged picks this. An antineutrino, like a neutrino, has no charge and negligible mass, as listed.
questions.explain: A positron has charge +e, as listed, but it has the same mass as an electron, about 0.00055 u, not about 1 u. A mass of about 1 u is that of a proton or a neutron.
questions.working: Correct values: α: +2e, about 4 u; e⁺: +e, mass of an electron (about 0.00055 u); ν and ν̄: 0, negligible. The positron's listed mass (about 1 u, a nucleon's mass) is the error.

questions.q: A nucleus has nucleon number A and proton number Z. It undergoes an alpha decay, and the nucleus formed then undergoes a beta-minus decay. Which expression gives the number of neutrons in the final nucleus?
options: A − Z − 3
A − Z + 1
A − Z − 1
A − Z − 4
optionWhy: After the alpha decay the nucleus has nucleon number A − 4 and proton number Z − 2. In the beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the nucleon number stays A − 4 and the proton number becomes Z − 1. Neutrons = (A − 4) − (Z − 1) = A − Z − 3.
A student who exchanges the alpha-decay changes, lowering the proton number by 4 and the nucleon number by 2, picks this. An alpha particle carries 2 protons and 2 neutrons: Z falls by 2 and A by 4.

A student who thinks beta-minus decay changes a proton into a neutron picks this. In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the neutron number falls by 1 and the proton number rises by 1.
A student who counts the emitted electron as a nucleon lowers the nucleon number to A − 5 in the beta-minus decay and picks this. The electron is not a nucleon; the nucleon number stays A − 4.
questions.explain: After the alpha decay the nucleus has nucleon number A − 4 and proton number Z − 2. In the beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the nucleon number stays A − 4 and the proton number becomes Z − 1. Neutrons = (A − 4) − (Z − 1) = A − Z − 3.
questions.working: Alpha decay removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons: nucleon number A − 4, proton number Z − 2. Beta-minus decay changes a neutron into a proton: nucleon number A − 4, proton number Z − 1. Neutrons = (A − 4) − (Z − 1) = A − Z − 3. Errors: alpha changes exchanged (Z − 4, A − 2) → A − Z + 1; beta-minus as p → n → A − Z − 1; electron counted as a nucleon (A − 5, Z − 1) → A − Z − 4.

questions.q: Carbon-14 nuclei decay by beta-minus emission. A student claims that carbon-11 nuclei must therefore also decay by beta-minus emission. Which is the best evaluation of the claim?
options: It is justified, since all isotopes of an element decay in the same way.
It is justified if the two samples are kept at the same temperature.
It is not justified, since isotopes of an element can decay in different ways.
It cannot be tested, since each nucleus chooses its decay type by chance.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the decay type belongs to the element picks this. Different isotopes of one element can decay in different ways, because the type of decay depends on the numbers of protons and neutrons.
A student who thinks conditions such as temperature control how nuclei decay picks this. Temperature affects atoms and electrons, not the nucleus; the type of decay is set by the isotope.

The type of decay is determined by the isotope, not by the element alone. Carbon-11 has 5 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8, so knowing how carbon-14 decays does not tell us how carbon-11 decays. (Carbon-11 in fact decays by beta-plus emission.)
A student who thinks the type of decay is random picks this. The time of each decay is random, but the type is determined by the isotope, so it can be tested by observing carbon-11 nuclei.
questions.explain: The type of decay is determined by the isotope, not by the element alone. Carbon-11 has 5 neutrons and carbon-14 has 8, so knowing how carbon-14 decays does not tell us how carbon-11 decays. (Carbon-11 in fact decays by beta-plus emission.)

questions.q: The energy-level diagram shows a parent nucleus and two energy states of the new nucleus it becomes. The parent nucleus undergoes beta-minus decay to the excited state of the new nucleus, which then emits a gamma-ray photon as it drops to its ground state. What is the frequency of the gamma-ray photon? Use h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s.
options: 1.6 × 10²⁰ Hz
1.2 × 10²⁰ Hz
2.8 × 10²⁰ Hz
1.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz
optionWhy: The photon carries the energy between the excited state and the ground state of the new nucleus: E = 0.66 MeV − 0 = 0.66 × 10⁶ eV. f = E/h = (0.66 × 10⁶ eV)/(4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s) = 1.6 × 10²⁰ Hz.

A student who thinks the photon is emitted by the parent nucleus as it decays picks this, using the gap from 1.17 MeV to 0.66 MeV, 0.51 MeV. That energy is shared by the electron and the antineutrino of the β⁻ decay; the photon comes afterward, from 0.66 MeV to 0.
A student who gives the photon all the energy released picks this, using 1.17 MeV. Only the last step, from the excited state at 0.66 MeV to the ground state, produces the photon.
A student who divides 0.66 by h without converting MeV to eV picks this. 0.66 MeV = 0.66 × 10⁶ eV, which makes the frequency 10⁶ times larger: 1.6 × 10²⁰ Hz.
questions.explain: The photon carries the energy between the excited state and the ground state of the new nucleus: E = 0.66 MeV − 0 = 0.66 × 10⁶ eV. f = E/h = (0.66 × 10⁶ eV)/(4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s) = 1.6 × 10²⁰ Hz.
questions.working: Gamma transition: excited state (0.66 MeV) → ground state (0). E = 0.66 MeV = 6.6 × 10⁵ eV. f = E/h = 6.6 × 10⁵ eV / 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV·s = 1.59 × 10²⁰ Hz ≈ 1.6 × 10²⁰ Hz. Distractors: 0.51 MeV → 1.2 × 10²⁰ Hz; 1.17 MeV → 2.8 × 10²⁰ Hz; 0.66 eV → 1.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

questions.q: A nucleus containing 15 protons and 15 neutrons undergoes beta-plus decay. How many neutrons does the resulting nucleus contain?
optionWhy: A student who has the directions of the beta decays reversed picks this, turning a neutron into a proton. In β⁺ decay a proton changes into a neutron, so the neutron number rises to 16.
In β⁺ decay a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino. The new nucleus has 14 protons and 15 + 1 = 16 neutrons; the nucleon number stays 30.

A student who thinks the positron is a proton ejected from the nucleus picks this: losing a proton would leave the neutrons unchanged. The positron has an electron's mass; in β⁺ decay a proton changes into a neutron.
A student who takes the nucleon number to be the number of neutrons picks this: 30 is the nucleon number, unchanged by the decay. The new nucleus has 14 protons, so it has 30 − 14 = 16 neutrons.
questions.explain: In β⁺ decay a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino. The new nucleus has 14 protons and 15 + 1 = 16 neutrons; the nucleon number stays 30.
questions.working: β⁺: p → n + e⁺ + ν. Z: 15 → 14; N: 15 → 16; A = 30 unchanged. Distractors: n → p (reversed) → N = 14; proton ejected → N = 15; A reported as N → 30.
